payload.name: Knowledge-Sharing Activity Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone does to share knowledge, teach, mentor, or help others develop, use concrete activity verbs when searching and supplement after finding one activity.
content: When a question asks how someone shares knowledge, teaches, mentors, or helps others develop, do not search only the abstract phrase 'share knowledge'. Run hybrid searches using concrete activity terms such as 'gives seminars', 'teaches', 'mentors', 'coaches', 'trains', 'workshops', 'presents', and 'helps others'.
Include memory kinds event and plan; knowledge-sharing actions are often stored as specific events or planned sessions rather than as general knowledge statements.
After finding one activity, run at least one additional search with a different concrete activity verb before answering, because a person may share knowledge in multiple distinct ways.
Stop after two or three distinct query attempts yield no new activity, and answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: Access retrieval misses memories of concrete knowledge-sharing activities (seminars, teaching, mentoring) when the question is phrased abstractly as 'share knowledge'. The agent searches only variations of the abstract phrase and does not target specific activity verbs, so distinct supporting memories are left out of the answer.

payload.name: Current-activity title retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is reading, watching, listening to, or playing (e.g., 'What novel is X reading?'), include activity-specific query variants and run a structured event search for that predicate before answering no information.
content: When the question asks what a person is reading, watching, listening to, or playing (e.g., 'What novel is X reading?'), include query variants that pair the person's name with the activity verb and the object type: 'reading novel', 'watching show', 'listening to album', 'playing game'.

If the initial hybrid search does not surface a memory with a specific title, run one structured search filtered to memory_kind=event, subject=<person>, and predicate in (read, watch, listen, play) before answering 'No information available'.
Stop after that structured search returns no relevant memory; do not expand to unrelated activities or topics.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what a person is currently reading, watching, listening to, or playing, the initial generic search often fails to surface the specific title because the memory may be combined with unrelated content or the predicate is not matched. This skill ensures activity-specific retrieval is performed before concluding no information.

payload.name: Affective Hobby Evidence Search
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a person's hobbies or interests, especially when explicit hobby lists are missing or partial.
content: When answering hobby/interest questions, also search preference memories using affective-emotion verbs: 'finds comfort in', 'brings joy', 'loves', 'passionate about', 'enjoys', 'happy when', because stable hobbies are often stored with emotional language rather than as a hobby list.
Prefer preference memories as evidence for stable hobbies; do not list one-off events (e.g., a single class, one DIY project) as hobbies unless the memory shows recurrence or an ongoing interest.
Run at most one or two affective-phrasing searches after the initial hobby search, and stop once the explicit hobby list is covered or no new distinct hobbies appear.

candidates.solves: Hobby questions often fail when preferences are stored using emotional language (comfort, joy, love) and when one-off events are over-listed as hobbies. This Skill guides retrieval to affective preference memories and filters out non-recurring events.

payload.name: Retrieve alternate focus areas for 'besides' questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides an explicit main activity (e.g., studying, work), search for other life domains such as relationships, hobbies, and social activities.
content: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides an explicit main activity (e.g., studying, work), do not stop at generic self-care or non-study queries; add targeted searches for relationship and hobby terms like 'partner', 'relationship', 'together', 'hobby', and 'activity'.
Include event and preference memory kinds in these searches, and inspect memories that mention the person alongside another name or a joint activity even if they do not literally contain 'focus'.
Stop after two or three distinct query attempts once a plausible non-primary focus area is found; answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides a primary activity (e.g., studying or work), retrieval can miss relationship and hobby memories if queries are anchored only to the negated activity. This skill guides complementary searches across other life domains.

payload.name: Enhancement Props Retrieval for Practice Questions
payload.description: When a question asks how someone enhances, improves, or creates atmosphere for a named practice (e.g., yoga, meditation, workout), and initial results show only routines or benefits, search for concrete sensory props before answering.
content: When a question asks how someone enhances or sets the atmosphere for a named practice, do not anchor retrieval only to the activity name plus 'enhance', 'improve', or 'practice'.

Run a follow-up hybrid search for concrete sensory/ambiance terms likely to appear in the answer, such as 'music', 'candles', 'essential oils', 'scents', 'incense', 'lighting', or 'atmosphere', combined with the person's name.
Include memory kinds 'preference' and 'event' in these follow-up searches; enhancement props are often stored as favorite scents/music or as details of a past practice event.

If the first search returns only routine or benefit memories, treat that as over-anchoring and run these concrete-term searches before answering; stop once the answer components are supported or after two or three diverse searches yield no such memories.

candidates.solves: Questions about how people enhance or improve a recurring practice often expect concrete sensory or ambiance props (e.g., music, candles, essential oils, scents) that are stored in preference or event memories. Retrieval anchored only on the activity name plus 'enhance/improve' surfaces general routine or benefit memories and misses these answer-bearing memories.

payload.name: Compound Activity Retrieval with Constraint Omission
payload.description: Use when a question asks for an activity or pastime combining a person's enjoyment with another condition (indoor, pet, another person), and initial results only match one side of the condition.
content: After the first search, run at least one follow-up query using only enjoyment/hobby terms ('hobby', 'enjoys', 'interested in', 'started', 'likes to') and deliberately omit all additional-constraint keywords such as indoor, pet, or the other person.
Include memory kinds preference, event, and plan in these follow-ups; a hobby can be stored as a routine, plan, or preference without mentioning the extra condition.

If a retrieved hobby can reasonably satisfy the extra condition (e.g., an indoor-friendly hobby or a hobby that can involve a pet), treat that as the best candidate; otherwise answer from the best available evidence and do not invent connections.
Stop after one such follow-up and one combination check; avoid further expansion.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an activity that a person would enjoy while also satisfying another condition, such as being indoors, involving a pet, or pleasing someone else, retrieval often over-anchors on the extra condition and misses the person's stored hobby or preference that is recorded without mentioning that condition.

payload.name: Opening or Launch Object Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is working on opening, launching, or starting, and initial retrieval returns only generic project or business memories, use opening-focused queries and require evidence explicitly naming the thing being opened before answering.
content: When the question asks what a person is working on opening, launching, or starting, include query variants with the person's name and opening-focused terms such as 'opening', 'launch', 'grand opening', 'preparing to open', and 'opening night'; add a domain term if the question or memory context suggests one (e.g., studio, store, restaurant).

Before answering from a generic 'business plan', 'project', or 'work in progress' memory, verify it explicitly identifies the object being opened; if it does not, run one additional targeted search combining the person's name with opening-focused terms and inspect event/plan memories whose predicate or object indicates a launch.

Stop after that targeted search: if it returns a memory explicitly naming the thing being opened, answer from it; if it still does not, answer no information or the best supported evidence without expanding further.

candidates.solves: Questions phrased as 'what is X working on opening/launching/starting?' are often answered from generic work-in-progress memories such as 'business plan' or 'project', even when a more specific memory names the entity being opened. This skill ensures retrieval explicitly targets the object of the opening and that the answer is grounded in evidence naming that object.

payload.name: Thematic focus retrieval for sessions and retreats
payload.description: Use when a question asks what the main focus, theme, lesson, realization, or takeaway was from a session, retreat, workshop, or event, and initial results show only the activity/event name.
content: When a question asks about the main focus/theme/lesson/takeaway/realization from a retreat, session, workshop, or event, do not answer with the activity name alone.

Run follow-up searches with reflective terms such as 'realized', 'importance of', 'focused on', 'learned', 'takeaway', 'theme', 'mindset', 'appreciate', 'present moment' in addition to the event terms.
Include event and preference memory kinds, since realizations/takeaways may be stored as events or preferences.
Stop once you find a memory describing the subject's realization or focus; if none appears, answer from the best available evidence.

candidates.solves: When a user asks for the main focus or takeaway of a past session, retreat, or event, retrieval often surfaces only activity/event names (e.g., yoga retreat) and misses stored realizations. This skill instructs the access agent to search with reflective/theme-oriented vocabulary and include event/preference memories, so answers reflect the session's actual focus rather than the activity label.

payload.name: Include plan memories for strategy and advice queries
payload.description: When a question asks what strategy, advice, or tip someone discussed, suggested, or offered, apply this before answering.
content: Do not restrict retrieval to event and preference memories; also include plan memories, which can store offers to help and recommended strategies.

If the first search does not surface a plan memory describing the advice, run at least one follow-up hybrid search that replaces generic question wording with concrete strategy terms (e.g., 'study plan', 'break tasks', 'planner', 'schedule', 'set goals') and keeps the people involved.
Stop once a plan memory directly answers the strategy discussed; do not enumerate all plans.

candidates.solves: Retrieval misses helpful advice or strategies when they are stored as plan memories rather than events or preferences, or when query wording is generic and does not include concrete strategy terms.

payload.name: Retrieve Activities Besides a Named Activity
payload.description: Use when a question asks what sports, hobbies, or activities a person likes/does besides, other than, in addition to, or apart from a named activity.
content: After the first search, run at least one follow-up query that omits the named activity and uses enjoyment/recreation terms such as 'enjoys', 'loves', 'fun', 'recreation', 'summer', or 'with friends'.

Include event memories and preference/state memory kinds; the additional activity may be stored as an indirectly phrased experience (e.g., 'had an awesome time surfing') rather than an explicit hobby list.
If top results still only mention the named activity, treat this as over-anchoring and run another query probing the person's other leisure activities before answering.
Stop after two or three distinct searches once a different activity is found or no new distinct activities appear.

candidates.solves: This fixes retrieval failures for questions asking what activities or sports a person likes besides/other than a named one, where searches stay over-anchored on the named activity and miss indirectly-phrased recreational memories.

payload.name: Infer advice from demonstrated activities and hobbies
payload.description: When a question asks what advice a person or people would give about a major life transition, challenge, or personal growth, search for their own stress-relieving activities and hobbies as evidence in addition to explicit advice memories.
content: If a question asks what advice someone would give about a major life transition or challenge and explicit advice searches return limited results, run additional hybrid searches using concrete activity/hobby terms the person has mentioned (e.g., hiking, painting, road trips) combined with their names.
Treat memories of the person's own hobbies, travels, and stress-relieving activities as evidence of advice they would give, even if the memory does not contain the words 'advice' or 'recommend'.
Stop once the retrieved activities cover the core claims of the answer or after two to three diverse activity searches per subject; do not keep expanding to unrelated topics.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what advice someone would give about a major life transition or personal growth, the agent searches only for explicit advice/recommendation memories and misses relevant evidence stored as the person's own hobbies and stress-relieving activities. This skill ensures those demonstrated behaviors are retrieved and used as evidence.

payload.name: Search Related Activity Terms for Complete Item Lists
payload.description: When a question asks for a list of items connected to a named activity, use this to also search related contexts and avoid stopping after one item.
content: When asked for a list of items (such as music pieces) associated with a named activity, run at least one follow-up search using closely related terms of that activity (e.g., for yoga: meditation, relaxation, calming, mindfulness; for workouts: exercise, cardio, training) and synonyms of the named activity.
Inspect preference memories returned under those related terms for concrete named items, even when the memory does not mention the original activity explicitly.

If the question indicates multiple items (plural, 'pieces', 'songs', 'books', etc.), do not treat the first matching item as the complete answer; continue searching until no new distinct items appear or the retrieved evidence covers all asked items.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a list of items (e.g., music pieces) associated with a named activity, retrieval often over-anchors on the exact activity and misses items stored under related contexts (e.g., meditation, relaxation), producing incomplete answers. This skill guides expanding the search to associated terms and continuing until the list is complete.

operations.name: Activity-Specific Verb Retrieval
operations.description: Use when a question asks what someone does, reads, watches, listens to, or plays, and initial retrieval misses concrete activities.

Run hybrid searches using concrete activity verbs such as 'gives seminars', 'teaches', 'mentors', 'coaches', 'trains', 'workshops', 'presents', 'helps others', 'reading novel', 'watching show', 'listening to album', 'playing game'.
Include memory kinds event and plan; these activities are often stored as specific events or planned sessions rather than general statements.
